Date: 2026-05-21
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Oliver Ruiz (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (EchoQuant CTO), Priya Nair (EchoQuant ML Eng), Sam Lopez (EchoQuant Infra), Marta Gomez (EchoQuant Product)
summary: POC scoping focused on capacity sizing for reserved GPUs, burst strategy, and fallback policies. Customer wants interactive answers for internal analyst workflows with p95 latency goal of ~250ms on short prompts and an exportable playbook for run-of-show. Discussed baseline workload, concurrency scenarios, expected cold-starts, cost delta for reserved vs burst, and trial benchmark cadence.
topics: Reserved GPU sizing vs burst capacity
Fallback model variants and quality checks
Security/ networking constraints for private POC
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Alex Rivera: Alex here, CTO at EchoQuant.
[00:08] Priya Nair: Priya, ML.
[00:10] Sam Lopez: Sam, infra.
[00:12] Marta Gomez: Marta, product.
[00:15] Ethan Park: Ethan here, I'll be the SE on the POC.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Great — objective today is to nail the POC success criteria, figure sizing for reserved GPUs for the pilot, and define burst/fallback runbook. We'll also capture next steps. Sound good?
[00:27] Alex Rivera: Yeah, high level — we have an internal analyst product where users hit a chat-like interface. Typical prompt lengths are short, 40-80 tokens, sometimes followed by a few-shot context of ~200 tokens. Concurrency spikes up to about 120 simultaneous users during reports. We need interactive latencies.
[00:44] Priya Nair: Right, and accuracy matters — we measure helpfulness with a small eval set. For POC we want no more than 8% drop in our eval score compared to our current runner.
[00:53] Ethan Park: Okay good specifics. Can you confirm current hardware/config you're running for baseline?
[00:58] Sam Lopez: We're running a mixed fleet on prem — mostly A100s for heavy jobs and some cheaper T4/GPU for prototypes. For this POC we'd consider Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity but also want to test a burst-to-hosted model for peak traffic.
[01:12] Maya Chen: So two-mode approach: reserve a base pool to cover steady-state concurrency, allow burst to Redwood hosted capacity or a higher tier reserved pool, and have fallback policies if burst can't be satisfied. We'll size the base pool to meet p95 latency target under your steady load.
[01:26] Oliver Ruiz: Quick note on model variants — we typically recommend using a quantized 8-bit variant for cost-sensitive workloads and keeping a higher-precision variant as fallback for quality checks. The runtime can do per-request routing.
[01:36] Priya Nair: That works as a pattern, but the eval score sensitivity to quantization is a concern. We need to run A/B trials during the POC.
[01:44] Ethan Park: Agreed. We'll include model variant regression tests in the benchmark plan.
[01:48] Alex Rivera: Can you outline how you calculate required GPUs? We want something we can validate quickly.
[01:53] Maya Chen: Sure, high level formula: estimated tokens per second * average token cost per GPU capacity -> gives tokens/s per GPU and you divide required concurrency*tokens_per_request by tokens/s per GPU. But we'll provide a worksheet. For your numbers: if average prompt+response is 300 tokens and you want 120 concurrent requests, that's 36k tokens in flight. If an A100 can sustain ~60k tokens/s for short-context generation with aggressive batching, that's roughly one GPU for steady state — but we need headroom for peaks and KV cache misses.
[02:25] Sam Lopez: Wait those token/s numbers seem optimistic. What's the batch latency tradeoff? We need p95 under 250ms.
[02:31] Ethan Park: Good question. For short prompts we recommend tiny batch windows (10-30ms) to preserve latency; that reduces batching efficiency. In practice we size for a conservative tokens/s per GPU of around 18k for low-latency scenarios on an A100; H100 can be 1.3x-1.5x better depending on kernel paths. We'll capture both numbers in the sheet so you can run scenarios.
[02:53] Priya Nair: So you're factoring continuous batching and KV cache hit ratios?
[02:56] Oliver Ruiz: Yes. If you have frequent prefix reuse (similar prompts), KV cache can serve many tokens from memory, boosting effective throughput. We want your traces to model that.
[03:05] Marta Gomez: About burst: EchoQuant has predictable weekly spikes when sales ops kick off reports. Those spikes can triple concurrency for 5-15 minutes.
[03:14] Maya Chen: For that short duration we often recommend a burst pool: reserved small baseline plus an ephemeral burst allocation that can come from shared capacity. Two flavors: (1) Redwood-hosted burst — fastest time to add capacity, pay-as-you-go; (2) reserved burst — you commit to a larger pool for predictable throughput. For POC we usually test hosted-burst first.
[03:33] Alex Rivera: And fallback? If hosted burst isn't available, what's the plan? We can't have timeouts.
[03:38] Ethan Park: Fallback policy examples: degrade model size (route to a faster, smaller variant), degrade response length/aggressively trim generation, or queue requests with progressive backoff and a graceful client error that shows stale cached answer. We'll codify the order: primary model -> quantized variant -> smaller model -> cached response -> error page.
[03:56] Priya Nair: Important: we need to ensure any fallback doesn't violate our accuracy threshold more than X percent. We'll attach acceptable deltas per response type.
[04:04] Oliver Ruiz: We'll support hard constraints in routing rules: e.g., don't route to smaller model for financial reconciliation queries, only for exploratory Q&A. You can tag routes.
[04:13] Sam Lopez: Networking — for private POC we need VPC peering and dedicated NAT windows. We cannot have data leaving our network for this pilot. Is private deployment an option?
[04:22] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem. For the POC we can run in your VPC or in a dedicated VPC with private peering. That adds ~5-7 business days for networking setup with our infra team. We'll need firewall rules and a test window.
[04:36] Alex Rivera: Security wise, SOC2 and KMS integration — we need to confirm key management and audit logs.
[04:40] Maya Chen: We'll share the SOC2 summary and KMS integration doc in the follow-up.
[04:45] Priya Nair: Benchmarks — what does a typical POC benchmark look like?
[04:48] Ethan Park: Two-part. (1) Synthetic load: run concurrency sweeps from 10 to 300 concurrent sessions to map p50/p95/p99 latency and GPU utilization. (2) Replay: replay your traces with real prompt distributions and measure model quality regressions, latency, and cost. We'll run multiple passes: baseline model, quantized variant, and fallback policy enabled. That gives you cost vs latency vs quality curves.
[05:12] Marta Gomez: Timeline for all this? We need a runbook to hand to operations.
[05:16] Maya Chen: Proposed POC timeline: Day 0-3: kickoff and artifact exchange (traces, eval set). Day 4-7: sizing + config + infra prep. Week of Day 8-14: benchmark runs and regression tests. Week 3: results review and playbook handoff. So roughly 3 weeks end-to-end for a typical POC. We can compress if EchoQuant prioritizes the week 1 benchmark window.
[05:37] Alex Rivera: Cost expectations? We need ballpark for reserved baseline + hosted burst.
[05:41] Ethan Park: We'll send detailed cost modeling, but rough example: an A100 reserved-equivalent node at low-latency profile might cost X per hour; hosted burst billed per token/second equivalent. For quick math: if baseline requires 2 A100-equivalents reserved, and you see 3x spikes for 10 minutes twice a day, hosted burst could be a few hundred dollars per spike compared to paying for 2 extra reserved GPUs continuously. We'll put exact numbers in the sheet.
[06:09] Priya Nair: On SLA — we need p95 SLOs for production, but for POC acceptance let's set clear success criteria.
[06:16] Maya Chen: Suggestion for POC success criteria: (1) p95 latency <= 250ms on representative short prompts under steady-state concurrency; (2) quality regression <= 8% on your eval; (3) cost within target budget X (you provide); (4) runbook documented with burst/fallback steps and a scheduled benchmark demonstrating the behavior.
[06:36] Alex Rivera: Sounds good. We'll provide the budget cap in the follow-up.
[06:40] Ethan Park: A couple operational notes — cold-start behavior: when requests hit a model with empty KV cache, first few tokens can be slower. Our runtime warmers can pin warm workers or pre-warm KV entries as part of the POC. That reduces tail latency for rare keys.
[06:55] Sam Lopez: Pre-warm sounds necessary for reports. How much extra capacity does warmers require?
[06:59] Oliver Ruiz: Minimal — usually 5-10% buffer, depends on how many model shards you warm. We'll model that in the sizing sheet.
[07:08] Priya Nair: Observability — we need per-route token breakdown, tracing and cost attribution to specific prompts.
[07:13] Ethan Park: Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route p95 and a heatmap of sequences. We'll enable request sampling and exportable traces for your telemetry system.
[07:23] Marta Gomez: Ok, let's recap next steps verbally.
[07:26] Maya Chen: Sure: Redwood will send POC sizing worksheet and cost model (Ethan), SOC2 and KMS docs (Maya), and a proposed benchmark script and runbook (Oliver). EchoQuant will share traces, eval sets, and confirm the VPC/peering window (Alex/Sam). We'll target the benchmark the week of June 1st.
[07:45] Alex Rivera: Agreed.
[07:46] Maya Chen: Anything else?
[07:48] Priya Nair: One ask — include a quick decision table for fallback choices and the expected eval delta so we can pre-approve routes.
[07:55] Ethan Park: Will do.
[07:57] Maya Chen: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[08:01] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcript quality: speaker overlap occasionally labeled; some product names may be transcribed as "Redwood Dedicate" or "Redwood Priave" in the raw export. Several numeric estimates noted as rough and to be validated in spreadsheet.
